newsitem.title: USA: De Kooning sells for record $15.6 million.
newsitem.headline: De Kooning sells for record $15.6 million.

text.p: The market for Contemporary art skyrocketed on Wednesday when "Woman," a 1949 painting by Willem De Kooning, sold for a record $15.6 million to an anonymous bidder at Christie's autumn auction.

The crowd gasped as the gavel sounded to end the furious bidding on the De Kooning, which was displayed at a number of the world's most prestigious museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Tate Gallery in London and the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.

"Happy days are here again," declared Christie's spokesman Christopher Burge following the sale. "It was a triumphant sale which set the all-time record, edging out the 1989 auction, which was at the top of the market."
The autumn Contemporary Art auction brought in $33,919,800, with 53 sold of the 61 lots offered.
"Tex!", a 1962 pop art painting by Roy Lichtenstein, sold for $3,962,500 to an anonymous bidder.
Another Lichtenstein painting, "The Forest," sold for $2,092,500 to an anonymous bidder at a Sotheby's auction on Tuesday.
A U.S. dealer paid $1,707,500 for Philip Guston's "Beggar's Joys," a record price for a Guston piece.

A private collector paid $882,500 for Mark Rothko's "Untitled." A U.S. dealer paid $772,500 for Robert Rauschenberg's "Shortstop." A private collector paid a record $750,500 for Hans Hoffman's "Gloria in Excelsis." An anonymous bidder paid the largest price ever brought by a Josef Albers piece, $662,500 for "Study for Homage to the Square: Despite Mist."
U.S. collectors and dealers accounted for 64 percent of the sale, Europe 21 percent, Asia 8 percent, and all others 7 percent.
Perhaps the most significant aspect of the De Kooning price was the fact that it brought the highest price for any piece of work at auction this year.
"It's the first time in living memory that a contemporary work has sold for more than an Impressionist or Modern work," said Burge.
